name: eight-hour-block-hourly-spacing-intermediate-reversion
rationale: 8h/8h (2026-10-04) had the smallest static-mix deficit at 500,000 JPY yet (-0.58 Sharpe) but only 16 trades, which no trade-count ratio will accept. Holding the composite for 8h while rebalancing hourly turns each block into a constant-mix allocation: with the target frozen, the only trades are those that restore the target weight after price drift, i.e. sell-after-rise / buy-after-fall. Willenbrock attributes the diversification (rebalancing) return entirely to such periodic rebalancing, and 2026-10-01's Kitron/Wengrowicz citation measured short-horizon reversal in crypto, which is the condition under which that rebalancing earns rather than costs. This should raise trade count well above 8h/8h while keeping the slow signal; 2h-block/1h-spacing (2026-09-28) is the nearest tried neighbour and used the shorter rsi42/bb60 horizons.

paper_reference.title: Diversification Return, Portfolio Rebalancing, and the Commodity Return Puzzle
paper_reference.key_claim: A buy-and-hold portfolio earns no diversification return; the diversification return arises from periodic rebalancing to fixed weights, which mechanically sells relative winners and buys relative losers. Quantpedia (Hanicova, 2021) reports a significant rebalancing premium for daily-rebalanced crypto portfolios 2018-2021.
paper_reference.pros: shirube's benchmark problem is precisely that a static (drifting) mix beats it; a held target with periodic rebalancing is the textbook mechanism by which a rebalanced mix can beat a drifting one, and it maps onto existing signal_block_secs/rebalance_interval_secs knobs with no code change.
paper_reference.cons: The premium is a multi-asset, low-frequency effect measured gross of costs (the crypto study does not model fees); here the second asset is JPY cash, the horizon is hourly, and at 50,000 JPY the 0.001 BTC lot floor (~25-27% of the portfolio) will refuse most hourly drift corrections, so the mechanism may only be visible at the diagnostic capitals.
